newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU tries to plug single market holes by 1999.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU tries to plug single market holes by 1999.

text.p: The European Commission, desperate to boost economic growth and create badly needed jobs in the EU, is preparing an ambitious plan to complete the bloc's single market by 1999 -- six years after the original deadline.

The European Union executive will present a list of measures to EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17 that it says should be adopted by the time the single currency is created by the end of the decade.

Its plan aims to remove remaining barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and people across national borders -- seen as essential if the EU is to catch up with economic rivals the United States and Japan.
"We are all convinced that the single market is far from having delivered its full potential," said EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti earlier this month.

The Commission -- at the time led by its dynamic French president Jacques Delors -- launched the single market programme in 1985 to create a huge domestic market to help European firms compete on world markets.
To keep up the pressure, the EU set a December 31, 1992 deadline for completing it -- and almost made it.

By that date around 260 of the original list of 282 legislative measures had been agreed, made possible by new EU rules allowing for more decisions to be taken by majority vote so that no country could veto single market decisions.
COMPLICATED ISSUES STILL UNRESOLVED
However, some of the most controversial and complicated issues -- such as greater tax harmonisation and the abolition of border controls on people -- were left unresolved.

"The single market is in one sense a very big success, and it has made a lot of difference to the way people do business in Europe," said Keith Richardson, secretary general of the European Round Table of Industrialists.
"But of course it is still not a fully functioning single market. It is not really comparable to the United States or Japan. Our feeling is that there is a long way to go."

Monti aims to create a new momentum and step up pressure on the EU to complete the 1992 single market project, which the Commission describes as "the most ambitious and comprehensive supply-side programme ever launched".
The action plan would involve mainly four areas -- services, taxation, and simplification and enforcement of EU rules.

"There will be a list of concrete actions to be completed by specified dates," Monti told a news conference. "The objective being that of having in place as much as possible of a well functioning single market by January 1, 1999."
Monetary union itself is seen as key to strengthening the internal market by removing currency-related obstacles to trade.
Stanley Crossick, chairman of the European Policy Centre, welcomed Monti's efforts.

"1992 was a project that fired the imagination and the tail end of it, however critical qualitatively it is, doesn't in fact attract the imagination in the same way," he said. "Therefore they are right to re-focus on this with the new action plan."
Economic figures suggest that the 15-nation EU greatly needs a shot in the arm. It has created only 10 million new jobs since the 1960s, less than one fifth than in the United States.

The EU's unemployment rate is 11 percent, compared with the U.S. rate of 5.4 percent, while its gross domestic product per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States, reflecting lower labour productivity.
FOCUS ON APPLYING AND ENFORCING SINGLE MARKET RULES
The EU executive does not plan new legislative proposals as it did in 1985.
Instead, the action plan will focus on the need to apply and enforce existing single market rules, for example those affecting government contracts, which account for 11.5 percent of the EU's GDP.
But some existing single market proposals still await adoption by the EU, for example in the areas of company law, taxation, financial services and the free movement of people.
A proposal to allow companies to set up as a European rather than as a national firm, for example, has been blocked for years by a dispute over rules on worker participation.
Monti is also eager to avoid fragmentation of new sectors, such as information technology and biotechnology.
Some evidence shows the single market, while incomplete, has helped to create jobs, boost incomes and lower inflation.

"The single market's greatest achievement has been the abolition of customs controls, which got rid of an estimated 80 million documents a year in the process," said Karl Von Wogau, a German member of the European Parliament.
"The resulting increase in cross-border competition has benefited consumers and monopolies have been eliminated."

The programme also boosted the freedom of individuals to move to another EU country to work, study or live, although it has not removed all border controls on people -- arguably its most visible failure.

According to a survey published by the European Commission last year, the single market has resulted in up to 900,000 more jobs, an extra increase in EU income of 1.1-1.5 percent, and a lowering of inflation rates of 1.0-1.5 percent.
SINGLE MARKET SHORT OF EXPECTATIONS
However, this falls short of the confident predictions made in a report by an expert committee chaired by Paolo Cecchini, a former senior EU official.
The 1988 Cecchini report forecast that the single market over five to six years would add 4.5 percent to GDP, reduce price levels by six percent and create two million new jobs.
This gap between prediction and reality is to some extent explained by the deep European recession in the early 1990s.
But it could also reflect the gaps in the single market. Monti noted that only 61 percent of the 1985 single market measures had been implemented in all 15 member states.
"Much insistence in the action plan will be on mechanisms for better enforcement," Monti said.

The Commission has lately gone out of its way to publicise legal action it has taken against member states that have dragged their feet, and last month proposed fines against recalcitrant governments for the first time.

Monti said people also needed to know more about what the single market means for them, noting that many individuals who have contacted the Commission about the project believed that a work permit was still needed to work in another member state.
"Probably the biggest remaining barrier to entry of the single market is lack of information," he said.
